prompt: Why can this course not be recorded entirely on a Linux computer?
hint: Think about who ships SwiftUI, and where it is allowed to run.

choices.text: Swift itself does not compile on Linux
choices.why: Swift does run on Linux: every transcript in the course was made there.

choices.text: SwiftUI and the simulator come with Xcode, and Xcode is licensed for Macs
choices.why: Right. The wall is Xcode and the SDKs inside it, not the language.

choices.text: An iPhone app has to be written in Objective-C
choices.why: Swift has been an app language since 2014, and the planner is Swift throughout.

choices.text: Linux cannot decode the JSON an app downloads from its server, so the network lessons fail
choices.why: Lesson 12 decodes JSON on Linux with the same Foundation an app uses.

prompt: Which lesson can be practised in full on Linux, with nothing left for a Mac?
hint: It is about talking to a server.

choices.text: Lesson 13, SwiftData
choices.why: SwiftData exists only on Apple systems, so lesson 13 is almost all read.

choices.text: Lesson 11, animation and transitions
choices.why: Only the arithmetic of a timing curve runs there; every animation needs SwiftUI.

choices.text: Lesson 12, URLSession
choices.why: Right: networking, decoding, errors and cancellation all run against a server on your own machine.

choices.text: Lesson 21, signing the archive with your team
choices.why: Signing needs Xcode and a paid membership; only the signing request runs on Linux.

prompt: A listing of SwiftUI code in this course has no output under it. What does that tell you?
hint: The course says what was run and what was not.

choices.text: The output was too long to print
choices.why: Long output is trimmed with a pipe that is shown; nothing is left out silently.

choices.text: It was written from Apple's documentation and not run
choices.why: Right. There was no Mac in the recording, so nothing from Xcode has a transcript.

choices.text: It ran, and printed nothing because views do not print
choices.why: Nothing from Xcode ran for the course; an empty output would be a claim of a run.

choices.text: It is an exercise left for you to complete
choices.why: The listings are complete code; what is missing is a machine that ran them.

prompt: How many gigabytes of disk did the unpacked Swift 6.4.2 toolchain take, according to `du -sh`?
hint: The line ends with the directory under `~/.local/share`.

prompt: `gpg --verify` printed `Good signature` and then a `WARNING` that the key is not certified. What should you do?
hint: Where did the key come from?

choices.text: Download the archive again, since the warning means it was altered
choices.why: An altered file gets `BAD signature`, as section 04 shows; this one matched.

choices.text: Carry on: the signature matched a key fetched from swift.org over HTTPS
choices.why: Right. The warning says you have not certified the key yourself, which is true and expected.

choices.text: Install the toolchain with `apt` instead
choices.why: Ubuntu does not package Swift 6.4.2; the course installs it from swift.org.

choices.text: Delete `~/.gnupg` and import the keys a second time
choices.why: Importing again gives the same keys and the same warning.

prompt: What do `-C -` and `--retry 5 --retry-all-errors` add to the `curl` that downloads the toolchain?
hint: The file is over a gigabyte.

choices.text: A dropped connection is retried and resumed from where it stopped
choices.why: Right: `-C -` resumes at the byte already on disk, and the retries make curl try again.

choices.text: The signature is checked as the file arrives
choices.why: curl knows nothing of signatures; `gpg --verify` checks it afterwards.

choices.text: Five copies of the file are fetched at the same time, so it arrives faster
choices.why: One file is fetched; five is the number of attempts.

choices.text: A failed download is deleted so it cannot be unpacked
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the partial file is kept so it can be resumed.

prompt: Match each command from section 03 to what it does.
hint: Two download, one checks, one unpacks.

pairs.right: Adds the Swift project's public keys
Checks the archive against its signature
Reads the new `PATH` line into the open terminal

prompt: You have a Mac with Xcode. What do you need to install to run this course's `swift build` and `swift test`?
hint: Xcode ships a compiler.

choices.text: The Linux toolchain from swift.org, inside a virtual machine
choices.why: Not needed: the Mac already has a Swift toolchain inside Xcode.

choices.text: Nothing: Xcode ships a Swift toolchain
choices.why: Right. The commands work in Terminal; only paths and the version line differ.

choices.text: Ubuntu's packages from the `apt` line
choices.why: That line is for Ubuntu; macOS has no `apt`.

choices.text: A paid developer membership
choices.why: Building and testing a package costs nothing; the membership is for lessons 21 and 22.

prompt: What exit status does the shell give when it cannot find a command?
hint: `echo $?` printed it in section 04.

prompt: `swift --version` answers `error while loading shared libraries: libncurses.so.6`. What fixes it?
hint: The message comes from the system's loader.

choices.text: Adding the toolchain's `usr/lib` to `PATH`
choices.why: `PATH` is where commands are found, not libraries; the library is missing from the system.

choices.text: Downloading the archive again and checking it
choices.why: The archive is fine: `swift` started and asked for a library the system lacks.

choices.text: Running the `apt install` line from section 03
choices.why: Right. It installs the libraries the toolchain links against, and it is safe to run twice.

choices.text: Opening a new terminal so `~/.bashrc` is read
choices.why: The command was found; a new terminal changes nothing about a missing library.

prompt: A friend's download was cut short, but `tar` happened to unpack part of it without complaint. Which check would still have caught it before unpacking?
hint: It compares the bytes with what the Swift project signed.

choices.text: `ls -lh`, since the file is smaller
choices.why: Only if she remembered the right size; nothing in `ls` says the file is incomplete.

choices.text: `gpg --verify` with the `.sig` file
choices.why: Right: any change to the bytes, a cut or an edit, gives `BAD signature`.

choices.text: `swift --version` once the toolchain is unpacked
choices.why: That runs after unpacking, and a damaged toolchain can fail anywhere later.

choices.text: `which swift`, to confirm the path
choices.why: It finds the program on `PATH`; it says nothing about whether the program is whole.

prompt: Why is `StudySession.date` a `String` like `2026-10-19` rather than a `Date`?
hint: A `Date` is an instant; a planned day has no time and no zone.

choices.text: `Date` is not available in Foundation on Linux
choices.why: It is: `Days.swift` uses `Date` and `Calendar` on Linux to find the Monday.

choices.text: Strings sort faster than dates in a list
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the reason is what a day means.

choices.text: A day read in the phone's zone could move to another week
choices.why: Right. As text it is the same day everywhere, and the calendar that reads it is pinned to UTC.

choices.text: SwiftUI's `DatePicker` returns a string
choices.why: A `DatePicker` binds to a `Date`; lesson 10 turns it into a day.

prompt: `week` printed the total for the week of 19 October. How many minutes were planned?
hint: Four sessions fall between the 19th and the 25th.

prompt: `plan.add` is declared `mutating` and `throws(PlanError)`. What does `mutating` mean here?
hint: `Plan` is a struct.

choices.text: The method may run on another thread
choices.why: Threads have nothing to do with it; lesson 12 meets concurrency.

choices.text: Every copy of the plan gets the new session
choices.why: A struct is a value: only the copy the method was called on changes.

choices.text: The caller has to handle an error
choices.why: That is `throws`; `mutating` is about changing the value.

choices.text: It changes the value it was called on
choices.why: Right, and so it can only be called on a `var`, as `week`'s `plan` is.

prompt: The manifest's first line, `// swift-tools-version: 6.0`, is read by the toolchain. It sets the manifest format and the Swift 6 language ___.
hint: The mode where a data race is an error.

prompt: In an Xcode project, what is a scheme?
hint: A target says what to build.

choices.text: What to do with targets: build, run, test or archive them
choices.why: Right. Run, Test and Archive act on the scheme chosen beside the stop button.

choices.text: A product to build, like the app, its unit tests or its UI tests, with its own settings
choices.why: That is a target; a scheme says what to do with targets.

choices.text: The colour theme of the editor
choices.why: Xcode calls those themes; a scheme is about building.

choices.text: A list of the package's dependencies
choices.why: Dependencies are in `Package.swift` and the project's package list.

prompt: Which build configuration does an archive for the App Store use by default?
hint: One compiles fast; the other optimises.

choices.text: Debug, to keep symbols for crash reports
choices.why: Debug is for development; symbols for crash reports are kept separately.

choices.text: Release
choices.why: Right: Release optimises, and Archive uses it.

choices.text: Whichever the simulator last ran
choices.why: The scheme's Archive action names its configuration; the simulator does not decide.

choices.text: A third configuration called Store
choices.why: A new project has two configurations, Debug and Release.

prompt: You change `weekTotal` in the package and run `swift test` in its directory, then build the app in Xcode. Which statement is true?
hint: The package is local, not a copy.

choices.text: The app keeps the old code until the package is added again
choices.why: A local package is read from its directory at every build.

choices.text: `swift test` cannot run while Xcode has the package open
choices.why: Both read the same files; neither locks them.

choices.text: Both use the same files, so the app's next build has the change
choices.why: Right. That is the point of the arrangement: one copy of the code, tested anywhere.

choices.text: The app must import `PlannerCoreTests` to see the change
choices.why: The app imports the library; the tests are a separate target.

prompt: Which of these may change in every release without making a different app?
hint: Think of the name under the icon.

choices.text: `CFBundleIdentifier`
choices.why: Changing the identifier publishes a different app.

choices.text: `CFBundleDisplayName`
choices.why: Right: the name people see is a label, and it can change.

choices.text: The team identifier in the App ID
choices.why: That is your developer account's, and with the bundle id it is the App ID.

choices.text: The widget extension's identifier prefix
choices.why: It has to start with the app's identifier, which cannot change either.

prompt: Which identifier would a widget extension of `com.example.planner` need?
hint: iOS ties an extension to its app by a prefix.

choices.text: `widget.com.example.planner`
choices.why: The suffix goes at the end; the app's identifier has to be the start.

choices.text: `com.example.planner_widget`
choices.why: An underscore is not allowed in a bundle identifier.

choices.text: `com.example.planner.widget`
choices.why: Right: it starts with the app's identifier, which is how iOS knows whose it is.

choices.text: `com.example.widget`
choices.why: That shares the domain but not the app's identifier.

prompt: A colleague registers `com.example.Planner` for a new app. Your app is `com.example.planner`. What happens?
hint: Read what the documentation says about case.

choices.text: The same identifier: case does not count
choices.why: Right. Case can never tell two apps apart.

choices.text: Two apps, since one letter differs
choices.why: Apple's documentation says bundle IDs are case-insensitive.

choices.text: The upload fails because capitals are not allowed at all
choices.why: Capitals are allowed; the rule lists A to Z and a to z.

choices.text: iOS installs both and shows two icons
choices.why: To iOS they are one app, so the second replaces the first.

prompt: You upload build 1 of version 1.0, fix a bug and upload again. Which key must change?
hint: Two keys are versions, and only one is the build.

choices.text: `CFBundleShortVersionString`, to 1.0.1, and nothing else
choices.why: You may raise the version, but the build number is what every upload needs higher.

choices.text: `CFBundleVersion`, to a higher build number
choices.why: Right: every build uploaded for the same version needs a higher one.

choices.text: `CFBundleIdentifier`
choices.why: Changing it would make a different app.

choices.text: `MinimumOSVersion`, to the iOS the new build needs
choices.why: That is the iOS the app needs, unrelated to the upload.

prompt: Which of these would `check.swift` report as a bad version string?
hint: Up to three integers separated by periods.

choices.why: Three integers, and 10 is an integer.
One integer is allowed: up to three means one, two or three.
Right: the doubled period leaves an empty part, and the split keeps it.
Three integers; a version may start at zero.

prompt: Put the install from section 03 in order.
hint: Libraries, download, check, unpack, path.

prompt: In `mondayOf`, `back` is `(weekday + 5) % 7`, where Foundation counts Sunday as 1. What is `back` for a Sunday?
hint: Work it out: (1 + 5) % 7.

choices.text: 0, so a Sunday counts as its own Monday
choices.why: 0 is Monday's value: (2 + 5) % 7.

choices.text: 1, so the Monday is the next day
choices.why: `back` counts days backwards, and a week here starts on Monday.

choices.text: 6, so the Monday is six days earlier
choices.why: Right: the test pins it, `mondayOf("2026-10-25")` is `2026-10-19`.

choices.text: 7, a whole week back to the Monday before
choices.why: `% 7` keeps it between 0 and 6.

prompt: Which of these runs on the Linux machine this course was recorded on? Choose all that apply.
hint: Plain Swift and Foundation run; Apple's SDKs do not.

choices.text: `swift test` on the planner's package
choices.why: Yes: section 05 ran it.

choices.text: `PlannerApp.swift`, with `import SwiftUI`
choices.why: No: SwiftUI has no Linux version.

choices.text: `swift check.swift Info.plist`
choices.why: Yes: Foundation reads property lists on Linux.

choices.text: The iOS simulator, from the Run button
choices.why: No: the simulator comes with Xcode, on a Mac.
